newsitem.title: USA: GM parts strike in Ohio threatens broad shutdown.
newsitem.headline: GM parts strike in Ohio threatens broad shutdown.

text.p: The third strike to hit General Motors Corp. in about five weeks threatened on Tuesday to force a broad shutdown of GM's North American vehicle operations and to affect other automakers that buy GM electrical components.

In Warren, Ohio, about 8,200 members of International Union of Electronic Workers Local 717 walked off the job at 18 plants operated by GM's Delphi Packard Electric Systems division just after midnight.

The plants produce vehicle wiring harness components and other electrical parts for nearly all of GM's North American-built cars and trucks. The harnesses are used to distribute electrical power and signals throughout a vehicle.

Analysts estimate that GM could begin shutting down factories by late next week. Much of the assembly work for the harnesses is done in Mexico, so GM has significant parts inventories now in transit to its assembly plants.
In March 1996, a 17-day strike by the United Auto Workers against two GM brake plants in Dayton, Ohio, forced GM to idle 26 North American assembly plants at a cost of $900 million.

Ongoing UAW strikes at GM assembly plants in Oklahoma City and Pontiac, Mich., thus far have cost the automaker roughly 43,000 vehicles, or $194 million in lost profits, said Burnham Securities analyst David Healy. GM continues to lose about 2,300 vehicles a day to the walkouts.

The Oklahoma City plant, idled since April 4, builds GM's new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars, while Pontiac, which was struck on April 22, is one of three GM plants that build full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks.

Meanwhile, Chrysler Corp. said Tuesday that a month-long strike at its Mound Road engine plant in Detroit will slash its second quarter profits by $450 million, or 65 cents a share. The dispute cost Chrysler production of 94,000 trucks, few of which it will be able to make up.

The main issue in all of the strikes, including the IUE dispute in Ohio, is job security. The union, among other things, has demanded that GM guarantee that it will not unilaterally move more jobs to Mexico, where the manual labour needed for wire harness assembly is much cheaper.
"We're trying to keep all of our people working so they have a place to retire from," Local 717 President Nick Border said.
Negotiations to resolve the dispute resumed Tuesday afternoon about 13 hours after the strike began.

"Our main focus is on the impact this strike will have on our customers, both General Motors and non-GM," Delphi Packard Electric said in a statment. "Any interruption either actual or potential, in the chain of supply to our customers poses a great risk to the retention and ongoing expansion of our business."
GM lists about 34 other car and truck makers worldwide as customers of Delphi Packard Electric, but not all of them use components from the Ohio plants.

Other demands by the electronics workers union include abolishing the bottom tier of the plants' three-tier wage scale, which pays new workers 55 percent of the top-tier wage. Local 717 members rejected a tentative pact in March, in part because it did not alter the wage scale.
GM shares fell $1.50 to $56.75 on the New York Stock Exchange, but analysts attributed the drop more to a downgrade of the stock by PaineWebber Inc. than to the strike.

PaineWebber auto analyst Michael Ward said in a research report that he cut his rating on GM stock to neutral from attractive in part because GM's second-quarter operating profits from North America are likely to fall from the first quarter, largely due to the strikes and excessive dealer inventory levels.

"GM's earnings continue to suffer from labour unrest, and it's our fear that at some point the market will become less forgiving," Ward wrote, adding that near-term news about GM is likely to be more negative than positive.

With about 25 GM plants still lacking local labour agreements and several union locals requesting permission to strike, Schroder Wertheim analyst John Casesa said he expects GM's labour woes to continue.
"This is part of a continuing process of resizing this company," he said Tuesday. "Until GM's costs are matched with the market there's going to continue to be this tension."
